summary:
I've been building out TheLongRest, a D&D platform I run for my own table, and the last stretch was a real playtest push: I imported a published adventure by pasting the text in and having the app derive NPCs, monster stat blocks, and prep notes from it, review each one, then apply — the source text itself gets deleted afterward so nothing gets warehoused it doesn't have the rights to keep. Getting the derivation right took a few passes: an early version of the writer would happily invent full stat blocks from memory for monsters that were only mentioned in passing, so I had to add a grounding step that catches anything not actually sourced from the text and demotes it to a stub instead.

I also shipped a bug/survey page tied to each game session, built for a real playtest with friends. The one design constraint that mattered: anonymous responses can't just skip storing a name — they need a separate "already responded" record that has no link back to the answer, so someone can't be identified by cross-referencing. Small thing, but it's the difference between "anonymous" and "anonymous until someone looks."

On the infrastructure side, I run a small home lab and built a fleet monitoring dashboard from scratch instead of reaching for Prometheus or Grafana — partly to actually understand what I was monitoring, partly because my machines have quirks off-the-shelf tools don't handle well (a GPU box where "high memory usage" is normal and by design, so a generic threshold alert would just be noise). It now tracks per-device power draw across four machines, with a 447-watt spike from a monitoring gap that had gone unnoticed for months — the kind of outlier a naive average would have quietly erased.

highlights.oneLiner: Adventure Import: paste published adventure text, derive NPCs/stat blocks/prep notes, review, apply, then delete source
Shipped per-session bug/survey feedback page with anonymous responses that can't be cross-referenced
Built a from-scratch fleet monitoring dashboard instead of Prometheus/Grafana, tuned to home-lab quirks
Tracking per-device power draw across four machines, caught a 447W spike a naive average would've hidden
